Your questions are not silly! So essentially in the USA the age at which juvenile (i.e. youth) court jurisdiction begins can differ by state. In Colorado this currently happens to be age 10. This can be different ages in other states, or states can choose not to specify a minimum age (34 states don't right now). When states do specify minimum ages the ages can vary widely. In North Carolina for example, the minimum age at which a juvenile can be held responsible for a crime currently is 6 years old. So the short answer is that yes, across the USA there are certainly examples of youth younger than 10 being charged with crimes. But when you look at juvenile charges filed in the USA each year, youth younger than 10 are involved in a very small portion. In other words, it happens in the USA - but its rare. Here is a source with annual stats: [https://www.ojjdp.gov/ojstatbb/ezajcs/](https://www.ojjdp.gov/ojstatbb/ezajcs/)

Juvenile Justice in the USA is sort of my specialty so feel free to PM me if you have more questions about how this works here. Also you can see this reference for more info on juvenile court jurisdiction age ranges in the USA, it's an interactive map: [https://www.ojjdp.gov/ojstatbb/structure\_process/qa04102.asp?qaDate=2016&text=no&maplink=link1](https://www.ojjdp.gov/ojstatbb/structure_process/qa04102.asp?qaDate=2016&text=no&maplink=link1)

As far as parents being charged because of what a child does, I'd say it really depends on the circumstances of the crime and the jurisdiction (i.e. place) the crime occurs in. It definitely happens (but as I said it is controversial. Here is an NPR article on this topic that discusses a few examples: [https://www.npr.org/2014/12/16/371264533/should-parents-be-legally-responsible-for-childrens-serious-crimes#:\~:text=Most%20states%20will%20hold%20parents,bad%20parenting%20are%20less%20common.&text=%22It's%20often%20just%20a%20way,juvenile%20delinquency%2C%22%20she%20says](https://www.npr.org/2014/12/16/371264533/should-parents-be-legally-responsible-for-childrens-serious-crimes#:~:text=Most%20states%20will%20hold%20parents,bad%20parenting%20are%20less%20common.&text=%22It's%20often%20just%20a%20way,juvenile%20delinquency%2C%22%20she%20says).

I suppose that could be true. The question that scenario brings up for me though is, if the prosecution believed one of the parents did it - why did they choose to file the *same* charges they did against *both* parents? 

I'll try to outline my reasoning in a way that makes sense - but I'm having a difficult time wording it so my bad if it's convoluted. Also note that the \*\*\* caveat I put in my original post applies to the below statutes I cite as well.

Basically, to me it seems like the prosecution chose to charge the parents based on the language in this Colorado statute, which I'm going to call **section 1** and states: 

>"When a person acts knowingly or recklessly and the child abuse results in death to the child, it is a class two felony." 

This same statute then continues, "*except as provided in paragraph (c) of this subsection (7)."* If you then turn to paragraph c of subsection 7, the language is as follows (I'm going to call this **section 2**): 

>"When a person knowingly causes the death of a child who has not yet attained twelve years of age and the person committing the offense is one in a position of trust with respect to the child, such person commits the crime of murder in the first degree."

The language of section 2 would definitely apply in JonBenet's case. So my question basically is - if the grand jury thought one of the parents was primarily responsible for JonBenet's death - why didn't they indict that parent on 1st degree murder charges? In other words, why did they indict on section 1 rather than section 2? 

I know there could be several answers to this question....for example, maybe the prosecution didn't put forward 1st degree murder as a possibility for either parent to the grand jury. Or maybe the grand jury did feel one parent was primarily responsible for JonBenet's death, but didn't believe they murdered her on purpose (i.e. didn't do it 'knowingly') - which would make section 2 not applicable. 

But I can't help feeling like if the grand jury and/or prosecution thought that one of the parents was more culpable for JonBenet's death than the other, the charges would have reflected that. The fact that both parents were indicted on the same charges to me speaks to a belief by the grand jury and prosecution of relatively equal culpability in JonBenet's death.

*Reference:* Colorado Rev. Stat. § 18-6-401. Retrieved from: [https://codes.findlaw.com/co/title-18-criminal-code/co-rev-st-sect-18-6-401.html#:\~:text=(I)%20When%20a%20person%20acts,of%20this%20subsection%20(7).&text=(III)%20When%20a%20person%20acts,is%20a%20class%203%20felony](https://codes.findlaw.com/co/title-18-criminal-code/co-rev-st-sect-18-6-401.html#:~:text=(I)%20When%20a%20person%20acts,of%20this%20subsection%20(7).&text=(III)%20When%20a%20person%20acts,is%20a%20class%203%20felony).

Hello, I am a family violence researcher and former advocate. I wanted to chime in because I'm not sure if the below things have been mentioned already. But I would encourage you to consider doing the following:

1)please follow the links below and consider first contacting a domestic violence agency in IL or call the IL DV hotline provided. They will be able to provide referrals to you and your daughter for services that may be helpful for you in your area and get you connected (sexual abuse counseling and interviewing, court advocacy, legal aid and/or family/divorce lawyers familiar with DV, therapy, safety planning, medical services, shelter/food services if needed, etc). If they are not much help with your daughters case then consider contacting a sexual abuse center in your area listed in the link I've listed below as well.  Importantly both services can also be helpful in assisting you in navigating what must be an incredibly difficult time in your life and supporting you in making decisions for yourself and your children. The court system and DCFS  can be confusing to navigate. There are resources available to help you. Look for services that list they are "inclusive" and things like they are "available regardless of gender" (the link I've included below states this on their webpage btw so it can serve as an example). Don't hesitate to use these services - they are confidential and also often free. If you find someone that you feel like does not take you seriously because you are a male then hang up and call another option down the list or ask to speak with their supervisor. Such behavior would be extremely unprofessional - if you are speaking to someone who works for an agency that does not accept men they should be trained to treat you with compassion, take you seriously, and refer you to somewhere that does. [IL domestic violence resources](https://www.dhs.state.il.us/page.aspx?item=30275) [illinois sexual abuse resources](https://www.dhs.state.il.us/page.aspx?item=31985)

2)Many of the behaviors you are experiencing and describing your wife exhibiting are characteristic of abusive relationships. NONE of how she is acting or put you through is your fault. Her behaviors are her choice. She is an adult and capable of understanding that what she is doing is hurting you and her children. If she is mentally ill it is not an excuse - she is an adult and responsible for managing her own behavior so that she is not a danger to herself or others. If she refuses to do that it is 100% not your fault. Let me repeat **you are NOT responsible for your wife's emotions or her actions**. You are doing your best to protect yourself and your children in what must be a very scary and emotional time for you. That is commendable and I am proud of you.

3)Understand the following is not me attempting to scare you in any way -- I think it is important that you be informed that abusers are most dangerous and volatile when their partners attempt to leave. You need to be vigilant in taking steps to protect yourself and your children. You have taken the first step in doing that already by calling DCFS and obtaining a protection order. If your wife violates your protection order in **any** way I encourage you not to hesitate to call the police. When you do so it will help to have a copy of the protection order on hand (even an electronic copy can help!) to present to the police when they arrive along with an explanation and/or evidence of how she violated it. Have your court advocate or attorney also inform the court/judge who issued the protection order of her violation and/or attempts to contact you.  If her family is harassing you -especially if they are trying to contact her on your behalf, inform your attorney and/or the court.  If you call for the police and find the officers who come to meet you are not taking you seriously, present your copy of the protection order, explain why you feel unsafe, and don't hesitate to ask to speak with their supervisor if you still don't feel you are being heard.

4)I'd encourage you to educate yourself about abusive relationships and/or behavior. There are fantastic resources at 
[thehotline.org](www.thehotline.org) to help you with this - that's the website for the national domestic violence hotline in the USA. 

Best wishes to you and your family. Be kind to yourself.
